title: Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Two Texts on One Lawn
subtitle: The Treaty of Waitangi debate, signing and signature voyages, Aotearoa New Zealand, 1840
intro: On 29 January 1840 HMS Herald brought Captain William Hobson into the Bay of Islands with orders to obtain British sovereignty over some or all of New Zealand with the free consent of its chiefs. Eight days later, on James Busby's lawn at Waitangi, more than forty rangatira of Ngāpuhi put their names or moko to a document written overnight in Māori by the missionary Henry Williams and his son. Through the autumn and winter of 1840 copies travelled the coasts by ship and on foot to about fifty meetings, and by September more than 500 rangatira, thirteen of them women, had signed, nearly all on the Māori text.

Almost none of the record is diary in the strict sense. The Crown's side survives as Hobson's dispatches, Busby's draft and Williams's certified retranslation; the missionaries' as letters and, above all, William Colenso's notes of the 5 February debate, which he published only in 1890. The rangatira's own words survive in a narrower channel still: speeches given in Māori, rendered aloud into English by Williams, abridged on paper by Colenso and officials. Every speech in this chapter is labelled as interpreted for that reason. Two Americans, the consul James Clendon and the visiting commander Charles Wilkes, give outside views within weeks of the signing.

The heart of the matter is that there were two texts. In the English, the chiefs ceded 'all the rights and powers of sovereignty' and were guaranteed 'exclusive and undisturbed possession' of their lands, forests and fisheries. In te Tiriti, the Māori text most rangatira heard and signed, they gave the Queen te kāwanatanga katoa, complete government, a word built on kāwana, governor, and the Queen confirmed to them te tino rangatiratanga, the full chiefly authority over their lands, homes and treasures. One reading holds that kāwanatanga conveyed sovereignty as the Crown intended; another holds that the rangatira agreed to share authority, keeping their own over their people. This chapter sets the texts and the spoken explanations side by side without choosing between them.

On 14 November 2014 the Waitangi Tribunal released its stage 1 report on the Te Paparahi o Te Raki (Northland) inquiry, He Whakaputanga me te Tiriti, The Declaration and the Treaty. It concluded that the rangatira who signed in February 1840 did not cede sovereignty, that they agreed to share power with the Governor over British subjects, and that Britain intended to acquire sovereignty but did not explain this to them. The Tribunal stated that the report drew no conclusion about how the Crown later acquired the sovereignty it now exercises, or about what the treaty means today.

Read together, the eyes show a negotiation conducted across a language gap by people with very different stakes: a governor needing a cession, missionaries vouching for him with their own credit, rangatira weighing a governor's protection against his power, a Catholic bishop securing a spoken promise, and foreign observers who already disagreed about what the signatures meant. Hobson proclaimed sovereignty on 21 May, before most of the sheets had come home.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian, as used by the British officials and missionaries. Colenso's account of 5–6 February was taken down at the time but published in 1890. The Waikato–Manukau sheet is dated 11 April 1840, though the meeting at Waikato Heads probably took place in late March or early April; such entries are marked as a range. Hobson's dispatch reporting the Waitangi signing is dated here only approximately.

eyes.name: William Colenso
eyes.role: CMS mission printer at Paihia, aged 28; set the type for the printed Māori text of the treaty
eyes.side: Church Missionary Society (Anglican), Bay of Islands
eyes.where: Busby's lawn, Waitangi, standing near the officials' table
eyes.authenticity: Colenso's notes were taken on the spot at Waitangi on 5–6 February 1840, but his account was published only in 1890 (Wellington, Government Printer), fifty years later, as The Authentic and Genuine History of the Signing of the Treaty of Waitangi. The rangatira's speeches reached him through Henry Williams's interpreting into English, and he abridged them. It is the fullest record of the 5 February debate and of his own exchange with Hobson on 6 February, but scholars note its late date and its author's later views.
eyes.bio: Cornish printer, later botanist, politician and Hawke's Bay missionary. On 5 February he wrote down as much of the speeches as he could catch through the interpreter; on 6 February he publicly asked Hobson whether the chiefs understood what they were signing. His account is the closest thing to minutes the debate has.

sources.title: Booklet, The Authentic and Genuine History of the Signing of the Treaty of Waitangi (MTG Hawke's Bay copy)
T. L. Buick, The Treaty of Waitangi (1914), quoting Colenso (online reader)

eyes.name: Captain William Hobson RN
eyes.role: Naval officer, aged 46; consul and Lieutenant-Governor-designate under the Governor of New South Wales
eyes.where: HMS Herald in the Bay of Islands; Waitangi; Hokianga; Waitematā
eyes.authenticity: His dispatches to Governor Gipps and to the Colonial Office were printed in the British Parliamentary Papers (1840–41) and are widely reproduced; they are a negotiator's reports, written to show the Crown's object achieved.
eyes.bio: Hobson had visited the Bay of Islands in HMS Rattlesnake in 1837 and came back with instructions to obtain sovereignty with the free consent of the chiefs. He ran the Waitangi and Hokianga meetings himself until a stroke on 1 March 1840 left the rest to deputies. His reports are the state's record of what it thought it had gained.

sources.title: Te Ara (1966 Encyclopaedia): Waitangi, Treaty of

eyes.name: Henry Williams
eyes.role: Head of the CMS mission in New Zealand, aged 47; translator of the treaty into Māori and interpreter at Waitangi
eyes.where: Paihia and Waitangi; later Port Nicholson and Kāpiti on the Ariel
eyes.form: dated certificate, letters and later account
eyes.authenticity: His certified retranslation for Gipps survives with the treaty papers; his own narrative of the translation was written years later and printed in Hugh Carleton's Life of Henry Williams (1874–77).
eyes.bio: A former naval officer turned missionary, Williams and his son Edward turned Hobson's English into Māori overnight. He read the Māori text aloud on 5 February and interpreted the debate, so every rangatira speech that survives in English passed through him. In May 1840 he carried a sheet south and took Te Rauparaha's signature.

eyes.name: James Busby
eyes.role: British Resident at Waitangi since 1833, aged 38; his house and lawn were the treaty ground
eyes.form: draft text, dated letters and later memoranda
eyes.authenticity: His 3 February draft and covering explanation survive in the treaty papers; his later published statements on what the treaty meant date from the 1850s–60s, when he had his own land claims at stake.
eyes.bio: Busby had organised the 1835 Declaration of Independence (He Whakaputanga) signed by northern rangatira. He supplied the draft whose three articles Hobson kept, spoke on land at the 5 February meeting, and called the chiefs forward to sign on 6 February.

eyes.name: Bishop Jean-Baptiste François Pompallier
eyes.role: French Catholic Vicar Apostolic of Western Oceania, aged 38
eyes.authenticity: His own history of the mission was written later in French (English translation, Auckland, 1888); the request he made at Waitangi is known chiefly from Colenso and the officials. Paraphrase only.
eyes.bio: Arriving at Waitangi in full canonicals, Pompallier unsettled the Protestant missionaries and impressed many rangatira. On 6 February he sought a public assurance on religious freedom, which Hobson gave and Williams read out in Māori.

sources.title: T. L. Buick, The Treaty of Waitangi (1914), online reader
The Spinoff (2025) on the speeches, after Salmond's 2010 report

eyes.name: Felton Mathew
eyes.role: Acting Surveyor-General, aged 38; came with Hobson on HMS Herald
eyes.where: Bay of Islands; then the Waitematā with Hobson
eyes.authenticity: His 1840 diaries, with his wife Sarah Louisa Mathew's journals, were edited by J. Rutherford and published only in 1940; they give a full and often critical account of Hobson's first months. No quotation used.
eyes.bio: Mathew spoke no Māori, which makes his understanding of the promises valuable: he took the chiefs to be keeping full power over their own people. He later chose the Auckland site and planned Russell.

sources.title: Dictionary of NZ Biography (1940) — Felton Mathew

eyes.name: James Reddy Clendon
eyes.role: Trader and United States consul at the Bay of Islands, aged 39
eyes.where: Witness at Waitangi; his house at Okiato
eyes.authenticity: His dispatches to Washington and letters to Shortland survive in US consular records and are discussed in the NZACL Yearbook (2004) chapter on his back-translation (the 'Littlewood document' debate).
eyes.bio: Clendon witnessed the first signing and quickly reported it to Washington. He obtained an English back-translation of the Māori text and judged its sense much the same as the English, an opinion that later fed a long argument about drafts.

eyes.name: Lieutenant Charles Wilkes USN
eyes.role: Commander of the United States Exploring Expedition, aged 41
eyes.authenticity: His dispatch of 5 April 1840 to the US Navy Department is quoted in the NZACL Yearbook chapter; his Narrative of the United States Exploring Expedition (1845) also describes the Bay of Islands.
eyes.bio: Wilkes arrived seven weeks after the signing and talked with settlers and chiefs. His verdict that the signers did not grasp what they had done is a sharp outside view, coloured by American suspicion of British expansion.

sources.title: NZACL Yearbook 10 (2004), chapter on Clendon (quotes Wilkes)

eyes.name: Te Kēmara
eyes.role: Rangatira of Ngāti Rāhiri and Ngāti Kawa, whose people held land at Waitangi
eyes.authenticity: His words survive only as Henry Williams's English interpreting, abridged in Colenso's notes (published 1890) and summarised by later historians; never his own written text.
eyes.bio: Te Kēmara opened the debate against the governor and closed it with a second, theatrical speech. He spoke for the people on whose land the meeting stood and who feared what a governor would mean for their standing.

sources.title: The Spinoff (2025) summary of the speeches

eyes.name: Rewa (Manu)
eyes.role: Senior rangatira of Ngāi Tāwake, Ngāpuhi; a signatory of He Whakaputanga (1835)
eyes.authenticity: Known through Williams's interpreting as noted by Colenso (1890) and other officials; English summaries only.
eyes.bio: Rewa had put his name to the 1835 declaration that sovereign authority lay with the rangatira. On 5 February he told Hobson to go home and said the Māori were the governors of their own land.

sources.title: The Spinoff (2025) summary of the speeches

eyes.name: Hōne Wiremu Heke Pōkai
eyes.role: Ngāpuhi rangatira, about 33, a baptised Christian close to the CMS mission
eyes.authenticity: His 5 February speech survives through Williams and Colenso; his name heads the 6 February signatures (signature numbering on NZHistory). His later letters of 1844–45 fall outside this chapter.
eyes.bio: Heke argued, with an edge some heard as sarcasm, that sending the governor away would leave Māori to the French and the rum-sellers. Called first by Busby on 6 February, he signed; five years later he cut down the flagstaff at Kororāreka.

eyes.name: Tāmati Wāka Nene
eyes.role: Senior rangatira of Ngāti Hao, Hokianga; Wesleyan-associated
eyes.authenticity: His speech survives through Williams's interpreting as recorded by Colenso (1890) and in officials' accounts; English summaries only.
eyes.bio: Nene's speech late on 5 February, with his brother Patuone's, is credited by many accounts with turning the meeting. He fought on the Crown's side against Heke and Kawiti in 1845–46.

eyes.name: Rev. Robert Maunsell
eyes.role: CMS missionary at Waikato Heads, aged about 30
eyes.authenticity: His meeting is documented by the sheet itself (dated 11 April 1840) and the officials' correspondence; the meeting date is uncertain.
eyes.bio: Maunsell held the Waikato Heads meeting with the only treaty sheet in English, sent by Shortland pre-signed by Hobson. He explained sovereignty as law-making power for the Queen while chiefs kept their land.

sources.title: NZHistory: Waikato Heads, late March or early April 1840

eyes.name: Te Rauparaha
eyes.role: Paramount rangatira of Ngāti Toa, based on Kāpiti and controlling Cook Strait
eyes.authenticity: His agreement survives as his mark on two sheets (Henry Williams's Cook Strait sheet and the Herald–Bunbury sheet), witnessed and written up by British officials; his own words are known only through their reports.
eyes.bio: The most powerful rangatira of the Cook Strait region, Te Rauparaha was the man Hobson most wanted. He signed twice, the second time protesting that he had already done so.

entries.headline: The Herald anchors in the Bay of Islands
entries.digest: Ten days out of Sydney, Hobson brought HMS Herald into the Bay of Islands carrying Gipps's proclamations and a staff that included Mathew and Shortland. He set to work at once on a treaty, a document he had not been given in final form in London.
entries.source_note: Te Ara 1966 'Waitangi, Treaty of'; NZHistory 6 February 1840 page.

entries.headline: Commissions read in the settlers' church
entries.digest: Hobson landed at Kororāreka and read the Queen's commissions and two proclamations in the church: one announcing his authority, the other declaring that land bought privately from Māori would not be recognised. Notices went out calling the chiefs to Waitangi.
entries.source_note: Te Ara 1966; NZHistory treaty timeline 1800–1849.

entries.headline: An English-only official watches the first steps
entries.digest: Mathew, who had sailed with Hobson, recorded the opening days of the new administration in his diary, often critically. Unable to speak Māori, he depended on what officials and missionaries told him the chiefs were being promised.
entries.source_note: Mathew diaries, ed. Rutherford (1940), as described in DNZB (1940) entry; exact entry dates not seen.

entries.headline: Busby supplies a draft with three articles
entries.digest: Busby judged the notes prepared by Hobson and his secretary James Freeman unsuitable and handed over his own draft, with a long explanation of what it meant. Hobson kept its three articles (cession of sovereignty, Crown control of land buying, protection and rights of British subjects) and wrote a new preamble.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Drafting the Treaty.

entries.headline: An English text arrives for overnight translation
entries.digest: Henry Williams and his son Edward received the English draft on the evening of the 4th, with the meeting set for the next morning. They wrote it in the missionary Māori the rangatira knew from scripture: 'sovereignty' became kāwanatanga, a word built on kāwana (governor), while chiefs were promised te tino rangatiratanga over their lands, homes and treasures. Williams later wrote that he had avoided English terms with no Māori equivalent.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Drafting the Treaty; NZHistory comment page on text differences. Williams's later account in Carleton (1874–77) not seen directly.

entries.place: Waitangi, the procession to the marquee
entries.headline: 'This won't do': the bishop takes the front row
entries.digest: As the officials walked to the marquee on Busby's lawn, Pompallier in his robes took a place close to Hobson. Colenso turned to his fellow missionaries in alarm; Richard Taylor replied that he would never follow Rome. The Protestant clergy then placed themselves beside or behind the governor so as not to be seen ranked below the bishop.
entries.quote: this won't do. We must never consent to this position.
entries.source_note: Colenso (1890), as quoted in Buick, The Treaty of Waitangi (1914), online reader.

entries.headline: Hobson asks the chiefs openly for their consent
entries.digest: Before some hundreds of Māori and settlers, Hobson spoke from notes and read the English text, explaining that the Queen wished to protect them and control British subjects. He insisted he was asking in public, not working on chiefs one by one, and promised that land unjustly sold would be returned.
entries.quote: I do not go from one chief to another.
entries.source_note: NZHistory 6 February 1840; Hobson's words as recorded by Colenso (1890), quoted in Buick (1914). Speech summary: The Spinoff 2025 after Salmond 2010.

entries.headline: Williams reads the Māori text and interprets
entries.digest: Williams read te Tiriti aloud and presented it as a covenant between the rangatira and Queen Victoria, an act of love from the Queen. Through the five hours of speeches he turned each rangatira's words into English for Hobson, and Hobson's into Māori.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: 6 February 1840; NZHistory: Drafting the Treaty.

entries.headline: Busby answers on land
entries.digest: Busby addressed the meeting on land, the sorest point. Speakers accused settlers of grabbing land, and some pointed at Busby's own holdings; he told them the governor would not take land and that dubious purchases would be examined.
entries.source_note: NZHistory 6 February 1840 ('Busby discussed land'); details of his remarks from secondary summaries (Spinoff 2025 after Salmond 2010).

entries.headline: Te Kēmara opens: go back, governor
entries.digest: The first rangatira to speak, Te Kēmara told Hobson, as Williams rendered it, that he did not want a governor over him. He pictured himself pushed down low like a worm while the governor stood high, and complained that the governor could have him seized. He ended by telling Hobson to go back.
entries.source_note: The Spinoff (2025) summary after Salmond's 2010 report, drawing on Colenso (1890); NZHistory 6 February 1840 names him among those asking Hobson to leave. Interpreted English only.

entries.headline: Rewa: the Māori are governors of their land
entries.digest: Rewa told Hobson, through the interpreter, to go home: the Māori were already the governors of their own land and had no need of another. He warned of what had happened at Sydney, where the original people had lost their land and been made to labour, and urged the chiefs not to sign.
entries.source_note: The Spinoff (2025) after Salmond 2010; NZHistory 6 February 1840. Interpreted English only.

entries.headline: Notes on a long afternoon of speeches
entries.digest: Colenso tried to keep up with the interpreter as speaker followed speaker: Moka demanding his land back, Kawiti rejecting governor and soldiers, Wai asking whether a governor could stop traders cheating on pigs and potatoes, Tāreha holding up fern root as a sign of what he would rather eat than be bribed. Supporters such as Pūmuka, Wharerahi and Rāwiri Taiwhanga spoke between them. He set down abridged English, not the Māori.
entries.source_note: Colenso (1890) as summarised in The Spinoff (2025) after Salmond 2010; sequence of speakers from that summary.

entries.headline: Heke: who then would protect us?
entries.digest: Heke argued that if the governor went away the rangatira would be left exposed to the French and to the rum-sellers. In a turn some listeners took as sarcastic, he said the Māori were like children who should let the missionaries choose for them. His was one of the speeches officials judged most influential.
entries.source_note: The Spinoff (2025) after Salmond 2010; NZHistory 6 February 1840 (Heke among influential supporters).

entries.headline: Nene: stay as father, judge and peacemaker
entries.digest: Nene told his fellow chiefs that the land had already gone to the Pākehā and that what they now needed was someone to keep order among the newcomers. He asked Hobson to stay as a father, a judge and a peacemaker, and to keep the promises made. His brother Patuone followed, holding two forefingers side by side to show the governor and chiefs standing as equals.
entries.source_note: The Spinoff (2025) after Salmond 2010; NZHistory 6 February 1840 (Nene and Patuone influential). Interpreted English only.

entries.headline: Te Kēmara's second speech: wrists crossed
entries.digest: Before the meeting broke up, Te Kēmara rose again, crossed his wrists as if handcuffed to show what a governor's rule would mean, and then parodied an English greeting to Hobson. The crowd laughed, and the chiefs went back to their camp to talk through the night.
entries.source_note: The Spinoff (2025) after Salmond 2010 (Colenso 1890).

entries.headline: A bishop in canonicals at the governor's side
entries.digest: Pompallier came in full robes and sat close to Hobson, which many Māori read as a sign of rank and which dismayed the Protestant missionaries. He watched the debate as head of the small Catholic mission whose converts included some Hokianga hapū.
entries.source_note: Buick (1914) quoting eyewitnesses; Colenso (1890).

entries.headline: Mathew's reading: chiefs remain independent
entries.digest: Mathew, who understood only the English, took away the impression that the rangatira would keep full power over their own people and remain independent under the Queen's protection. His diary records the meeting as a British official understood it.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Drafting the Treaty, citing Mathew's journal (ed. Rutherford, 1940); the entry date is inferred.

entries.headline: Called back a day early, in plain clothes
entries.digest: Hobson had expected the chiefs to take until the 7th, but food was short and they wanted the business done. Summoned at short notice, he came in plain clothes with his plumed hat, refused further debate because the meeting had not been formally called, and said he would take the signatures of any who chose to sign. After each one he shook hands and said, in Māori, 'He iwi tahi tātou', we are now one people.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Signing the Treaty; NZHistory 6 February 1840. The handshake phrase rests mainly on Colenso (1890) and is questioned by some writers (newzealandwars.co.nz essay).

entries.headline: A promise on religion, read aloud
entries.digest: Pompallier asked Hobson for an assurance that the Catholic faith would be protected. Hobson agreed, and Williams read a statement in Māori that the governor would protect the faiths of England, of the Wesleyans and of Rome, and also Māori custom. It was never written into the treaty text, and is sometimes called the 'fourth article'.
entries.source_note: The Spinoff (2025) after Salmond 2010; Colenso (1890).

entries.headline: Busby calls the chiefs forward
entries.digest: Busby read out the names of the rangatira to come and sign, beginning with Hōne Heke Pōkai. About half of those who signed that day had also signed his 1835 Declaration of Independence.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Signing the Treaty.

entries.headline: Heke signs first
entries.digest: Called first by Busby, Heke wrote his name on the Waitangi sheet. Others followed, some after fierce speeches against signing; Marupō and Ruhe spoke hotly and then signed. By evening about 40 to 46 rangatira had signed (sources differ).
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Signing the Treaty and 6 February 1840 (43 signatures, number disputed; Te Ara 1966 gives 45).

entries.headline: Colenso asks: do they understand?
entries.digest: As the signing began, Colenso asked leave to speak and told Hobson he doubted the chiefs understood what they were signing or the articles of the treaty, and that they might later hold the missionaries responsible. As Colenso recorded it, Hobson answered that he had done what he could to explain it and that if they did not understand it was not his fault. The signing went on.
entries.source_note: Colenso (1890) as paraphrased by NZHistory sources and newzealandwars.co.nz; exact words not quoted here because the original page was not seen.

entries.headline: The American consul signs as witness
entries.digest: Clendon stood among the European witnesses to the first signatures. As consul of a rival power he had a direct interest in what Britain was acquiring and how firmly.
entries.source_note: NZACL Yearbook 10 (2004), Clendon chapter.

entries.headline: Williams certifies a translation back into English
entries.digest: Around the time of the signing Williams made an English rendering of the Māori text for Governor Gipps and signed a note certifying that it was as literal a translation as Māori idiom allowed. Read beside Hobson's English, it shows where the texts part company.
entries.quote: as the idiom of the language will allow
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Signing the Treaty and 'Gathering signatures' page.

entries.headline: Hobson reports a clear recognition of sovereignty
entries.digest: Hobson reported the day's signatures to Gipps and to London as a full recognition of the Queen's sovereign rights over the northern part of the country. His dispatches said little about the conditions the chiefs had spoken of.
entries.quote: must be deemed a full and clear recognition of the sovereign-rights
entries.source_note: Te Ara 1966 quotes the phrase from Hobson's dispatch; the exact dispatch date is not confirmed here.

entries.headline: Six more signatures inland
entries.digest: Williams witnessed, with Captain Nias, the signatures of six Ngāpuhi rangatira at the Waimate mission, where some who had signed on the 6th encouraged others. No explanation of the treaty is recorded there; the party was passing through to Hokianga and stayed with Richard Taylor.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Waimate North, 9–10 February 1840.

entries.headline: An 'unfavourable spirit' at Hokianga
entries.digest: Several thousand people gathered at Māngungu. Hobson found the morning mood hostile; opponents spoke first, Pāpāhia comparing the governor to a high mountain and the chiefs to low hills, Taonui saying land was a parent and would not be given up. Hobson, interpreted by the Wesleyan John Hobbs, promised land would never be taken by force. Sixty-four signatures were added between 6 p.m. and midnight.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Māngungu, 12 February 1840 (citing Hobson's account).

entries.headline: Hokianga leaders and the treaty
entries.digest: Nene's own district debated the treaty at Māngungu, with Wesleyan missionaries urging it as good for Māori. Those who signed there, led by Nene, Āperahama Taonui and Mohi Tāwhai, became the Crown's firmest Māori allies in the north.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Māngungu, 12 February 1840; Nene's personal role on this day not separately documented in the sources seen.

entries.headline: Two hapū ask to take their names off
entries.digest: After a day of feasting and blanket-giving at Hōreke, rangatira of two Catholic hapū asked to be withdrawn from the treaty, and another hapū sent back its blankets with a letter of 50 names. Hobson would not strike any signature out.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Māngungu, 12 February 1840.

entries.headline: 200 printed copies of te Tiriti
entries.digest: The CMS press at Paihia, which Colenso ran, printed 200 copies of the Māori text for circulation round the country. It was the text most rangatira would hear read, and the one most of them signed.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Signing the Treaty and 'Gathering signatures' (200 copies, 17 February); Colenso's role as the mission printer is standard.

entries.headline: Consul's dispatch: the rest will follow
entries.digest: Clendon told Washington that many chiefs had already signed and the rest were expected to. He enclosed or obtained an English back-translation of the Māori text and noted that its sense was much the same as the English, though the words differed.
entries.quote: Many chiefs have signed this Treaty
entries.source_note: Clendon, Despatch no. 6, 20 February 1840, quoted in NZACL Yearbook 10 (2004).

entries.headline: Looking for a capital on the Waitematā
entries.digest: Mathew went with Hobson to the Waitematā to look for a seat of government. He judged the isthmus the key to the whole country, an opinion that led to the founding of Auckland later that year.
entries.source_note: DNZB (1940) entry on Felton Mathew; Te Ara 1966 (Hobson at the Waitematā, 21 February).

entries.headline: Hobson's stroke halts the tour
entries.digest: Hobson suffered a stroke and was taken back to the Bay of Islands. Signing copies were handed to Colonial Secretary Shortland, officers and missionaries to collect agreement around the country.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Signing the Treaty; Te Ara 1966.

entries.headline: Clendon asks for an official copy
entries.digest: Clendon wrote to Shortland asking for an authenticated copy of the treaty to send to the United States government.
entries.source_note: NZACL Yearbook 10 (2004), Clendon chapter.

entries.date_display: Late March or early April 1840 (sheet dated 11 April)
entries.headline: 1,500 gather; an English sheet is signed
entries.digest: Maunsell, instructed by letter from Shortland, held a meeting attended by about 1,500 people with the only sheet in English, pre-signed by Hobson and dated 6 February. He explained sovereignty as the Queen's power to make laws while the rangatira kept their land. Thirty-two rangatira of Waikato, Ngāti Maniapoto, Ngāti Raukawa and Ngāti Hauā signed; with no gifts to hand out, some were about to destroy the sheet until W. C. Symonds arrived with blankets on 3 April.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Waikato Heads, late March or early April 1840; meeting date uncertain.

entries.headline: An American captain doubts the signers knew
entries.digest: A week after arriving, Wilkes reported to his government that the chiefs who had signed did not understand the act they had performed. He wrote as a sceptical outsider who had spoken with settlers and some chiefs.
entries.quote: not aware of the act they have done
entries.source_note: Wilkes, Despatch no. 64, 5 April 1840, quoted in NZACL Yearbook 10 (2004).

entries.headline: Te Rauparaha the 'principal object'
entries.digest: Hobson told Henry Williams that the chief aim of his voyage south was Te Rauparaha's agreement, which he believed would give the Crown undisputed sovereignty over the southern districts.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Kāpiti, 14 May 1840 (quoting Hobson's instructions to Williams); date of the instruction not given.

entries.headline: Te Rauparaha's mark on the Cook Strait sheet
entries.digest: Arriving on the Ariel from the top of the South Island, Williams took four signatures at Kāpiti: Te Rauparaha, his son Tāmihana, Hēnare Mātene Te Whiwhi and Rangi Topeora, Te Rauparaha's niece, one of the 13 women known to have signed. Octavius Hadfield witnessed them.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Kāpiti, 14 May 1840.

entries.headline: Te Rauparaha signs at Kāpiti
entries.digest: Te Rauparaha made his own distinctive mark beside the name Williams wrote for him. What he understood himself to be agreeing to was not recorded in his own words; British officials took his signature as covering the Cook Strait region.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Kāpiti, 14 May 1840.

entries.headline: Two proclamations: cession and discovery
entries.digest: Before most of the sheets had come back, Hobson proclaimed the Queen's sovereignty over the North Island on the grounds of cession by the chiefs, and over the South and Stewart Islands on the grounds of discovery. He may have been hurried by reports that the New Zealand Company settlers at Port Nicholson were setting up their own government. He sent the proclamations to London on 25 May.
entries.source_note: Te Ara 1966; NZHistory treaty timeline 1800–1849.

entries.headline: Signing a second time on the Herald
entries.digest: When Major Bunbury met him off Mana, Te Rauparaha said he had already signed Williams's copy, but Bunbury insisted he sign the Herald sheet as well, which he did; Te Rangihaeata was brought aboard and signed too. Two days earlier Bunbury had proclaimed sovereignty over the South Island at Cloudy Bay.
entries.source_note: NZHistory: Herald (Bunbury) sheet, 19 June 1840; timeline for 17 June proclamation.

entries.headline: Fifty years on, Colenso publishes his notes
entries.digest: For the treaty's jubilee Colenso published his notes as The Authentic and Genuine History of the Signing of the Treaty of Waitangi. It fixed the popular picture of the debate and of Hobson's 'one people', but it was printed half a century after the event by a man with his own causes.
entries.source_note: MTG Hawke's Bay catalogue record of the booklet; newzealandwars.co.nz essay on its date.

claims.claim: Land bought privately from Māori will not be recognised without Crown title; Hobson's authority proclaimed
claims.evidence: Proclamations read at Kororāreka (Te Ara 1966; NZHistory timeline)

Land will 'never be forcibly taken'; Crown will act with truth and justice

convergences.label: The night of translation
convergences.note: Busby's draft, Hobson's preamble and the Williamses' overnight Māori meet in one text; what the English called sovereignty, the Māori called kāwanatanga.

convergences.label: The debate on Busby's lawn
convergences.note: Ten vantage points on one afternoon: the governor's assurances, the interpreter's renderings, the printer's notes, opponents telling Hobson to go, supporters asking him to stay as a father, a bishop at the table, and an English-only official who heard 'independent'.

convergences.label: Signing at Waitangi
convergences.note: Busby calls the names, Heke signs first, Pompallier gains a spoken promise, Colenso questions understanding, and the American consul watches as witness; Hobson reports a full recognition of sovereignty.

convergences.label: Māngungu, Hokianga
convergences.note: Hobson's 'unfavourable spirit' and the promise of no forcible taking, set beside the Hokianga leaders who became the Crown's firmest allies.

convergences.label: Foreign eyes on the treaty
convergences.note: The resident American consul thinks the sense of both texts much the same and expects all to sign; the visiting American commander thinks the signers did not know what they had done.

convergences.label: Kāpiti and the southern prize
convergences.note: Hobson's 'principal object', Williams's four signatures and Te Rauparaha's own mark: three records of one agreement, none in Te Rauparaha's words.

convergences.label: Proclamation before the sheets came home
convergences.note: Hobson proclaimed sovereignty while sheets were still travelling; Te Rauparaha signed again in June, and the last known name was added at Kāwhia on 3 September.

ties.note: Williams translated Hobson's English and interpreted for him at Waitangi, then carried a sheet south on his instructions.
Busby supplied the draft Hobson adapted and hosted the meeting at his residence.
On 6 February Colenso challenged Hobson in public over whether the chiefs understood the treaty.
Colenso objected to the bishop's place beside the governor and recorded the religious assurance given at his request.
Colenso's English record of the rangatira speeches is his note of Williams's interpreting; both were CMS men at Paihia.
Te Kēmara opened the case against the governor; Heke argued he should stay and signed first.
Rewa had signed Busby's 1835 Declaration of Independence and invoked the chiefs' own government against Hobson.
Both spoke for the treaty in 1840; by 1845–46 Nene fought for the Crown against Heke in the Northern War.
Two Americans reached opposite judgments within six weeks: Clendon that the texts agreed in sense, Wilkes that the signers did not understand.
Williams wrote Te Rauparaha's name on the Cook Strait sheet at Kāpiti on 14 May 1840.
Mathew sailed with Hobson on the Herald and was with him at the Waitematā shortly before his stroke.
Maunsell's sheet was Hobson's English text, pre-signed by him and dated 6 February, sent via Shortland.

threads_out.note: Hobson commanded HMS Rattlesnake when it carried Governor Bourke to Port Phillip in 1837, after Bourke had voided John Batman's 1835 'treaty' (Hobsons Bay is named for him). Gipps's January 1840 proclamation against private land purchases in New Zealand, which Hobson read at Kororāreka, applied the same doctrine.

The 1966 Te Ara account of the treaty begins with Cook's 1769–70 claim of possession in the name of George III, a claim the Crown did not rely on in 1840 when it chose to seek cession from the rangatira for the North Island.
Charles Wilkes, who doubted the Waitangi signers in April 1840, later commanded USS San Jacinto in the November 1861 Trent affair, seizing two Confederate envoys from a British ship.
